title: Bidirectional BFS in Nantes: The Fastest Way!
description: Watch Bidirectional BFS carve two expanding frontiers across a street-like graph until they meet. It dramatically reduces explored nodes compared to single-source BFS, making shortest-path visualization feel instant.
ig_caption:
🚦 NANTES on the map, but solved like a graph! 

Bidirectional BFS expands from the start and the goal simultaneously, using two synchronized queues. 🧠 In graph theory terms, you’re performing a meet-in-the-middle search where both BFS wavefronts progress level by level, guaranteeing a shortest path in an unweighted graph when the frontiers intersect. 

🌍 On a real street-map style graph (nodes as intersections, edges as walkable segments), this cuts the explored region roughly from O(b^d) to about O(b^(d/2) + b^(d/2)), where b is the branching factor and d is the shortest-path depth. ⚡

Want me to visualize the frontier meeting point and the final reconstructed route? Comment “BIDIR” and follow for more real-map algorithms! 🔁✨
fb_caption:
📍 Nantes (Île de Nantes) + graph search = ⚡ Bidirectional BFS!

This visualization shows how Bidirectional BFS runs two BFS searches at once—one from the start and one from the goal—until their frontiers meet. In unweighted street-map graphs, that “meet in the middle” approach finds a shortest path while exploring far fewer nodes than traditional single-direction BFS.
